\chapter{Las consecuencias}
\label{ch:es-las-consecuencias}
\hlchaptermodality{582}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say what follows from something, what it involves and what impact it had.}

Complete the last lesson of chapter 582: I can say what follows from something, what it involves and what impact it had.

\section[la consecuencia]{la consecuencia — the consequence}

\label{lesson:ES-C582-consecuencia}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for because of, then the Spanish for thanks to.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: la consecuencia}
\textbf{la consecuencia} — \textquotedblleft{}the consequence\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Todo lo que haces tiene consecuencias.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{Everything you do has consequences.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Como consecuencia} — as a result.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{consecuencia} is a learned borrowing from Latin \emph{consequentia}, built on \emph{consequi} 'to follow closely' (EtymDB).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{la consecuencia}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{la consecuencia}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{la consecuencia}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for because of, then the Spanish for thanks to, then say \emph{la consecuencia} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does la consecuencia mean? (\textquotedblleft{}The consequence\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el impacto]{el impacto — the impact}

\label{lesson:ES-C582-impacto}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for thanks to, then the Spanish for the consequence.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: el impacto}
\textbf{el impacto} — \textquotedblleft{}the impact\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
La noticia tuvo un gran impacto.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The news had a big impact.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Tener impacto en} — to have an impact on.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{impacto} is a learned borrowing from Latin \emph{impactus} 'struck against' (EtymDB), the participle of \emph{impingere}, built on \emph{pangere} 'to fasten, to drive in'.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}

\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{el impacto}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{el impacto}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{el impacto}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for thanks to, then the Spanish for the consequence, then say \emph{el impacto} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does el impacto mean? (\textquotedblleft{}The impact\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.

\section[conllevar]{conllevar — to involve, to entail}

\label{lesson:ES-C582-conllevar}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for the consequence, then the Spanish for the impact.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: conllevar}
\textbf{conllevar} — \textquotedblleft{}to involve, to entail\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Este trabajo conlleva mucha responsabilidad.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{This job involves a lot of responsibility.}
\end{quote}

Formal. It is conjugated like \emph{llevar}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{conllevar} is built on \emph{llevar} with the prefix \emph{con-}; \emph{llevar} is inherited from Latin \emph{levare} 'to lift, to raise' (EtymDB).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}

\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{conllevar}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{conllevar}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{conllevar}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for the consequence, then the Spanish for the impact, then say \emph{conllevar} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]

\section[por consiguiente]{por consiguiente — consequently, therefore}

\label{lesson:ES-C582-por-consiguiente}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for the impact, then the Spanish for to involve.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: por consiguiente}
\textbf{por consiguiente} — \textquotedblleft{}consequently, therefore\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
No hay tren; por consiguiente, vamos en coche.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{There is no train; therefore, we are going by car.}
\end{quote}

Formal; in speech people say \emph{por eso} or \emph{así que}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{por consiguiente} is built on \emph{consiguiente}, inherited from Latin \emph{consequentem} 'following', from \emph{consequi} 'to follow' (EtymDB).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{por consiguiente}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{por consiguiente}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{por consiguiente}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for the impact, then the Spanish for to involve, then say \emph{por consiguiente} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does por consiguiente mean? (\textquotedblleft{}Consequently, therefore\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[de modo que]{de modo que — so; so that}

\label{lesson:ES-C582-de-modo-que}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for to involve, then the Spanish for consequently.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: de modo que}
\textbf{de modo que} — \textquotedblleft{}so; so that\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Estoy cansado, de modo que me voy.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{I am tired, so I am leaving.}
\end{quote}

With the indicative it gives a result; with the subjunctive a purpose.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{de modo que} is built on \emph{modo}, inherited from Latin \emph{modus} 'measure, manner' (EtymDB).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{de modo que}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{de modo que}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{de modo que}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for to involve, then the Spanish for consequently, then say \emph{de modo que} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does de modo que mean? (\textquotedblleft{}So; so that\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
